notes: PNC governs alone since the December 1968 election (the PNC-UF coalition ended then), so there is no real coalition partner. The PPP, the main opposition and second-largest party, is placed in slot 18 (starting popularity) instead of MD slot 5; its pro-Soviet youth wing PYO holds slot 4. Brindley Benn's Maoist WPVP in slot 19. Slot 23 is the Guyanese Crown, still in place on 1 Jan 1970 (republic proclaimed 23 Feb 1970).

0.name: Special Branch of the Guyana Police Force
0.english: Special Branch of the Guyana Police Force
0.text:
The Special Branch is the political intelligence arm of the Guyana Police Force, built up under British rule during the turbulent years of 1953 to 1964. It kept files on the PPP, the unions and the radical students, and worked closely with British and American intelligence while Cheddi Jagan was in power.

Its officers see communism as the main threat to Guyana and favour firm executive power, surveillance and cooperation with Washington and London. They answer now to the PNC government, which finds their files useful against Jagan's party. Their leverage lies in information, in the police hierarchy and in their foreign contacts.

1.name: United Force
1.text:
The United Force was founded in 1960 by the brewer and businessman Peter D'Aguiar. It entered government with Forbes Burnham's PNC in 1964, helping to remove Cheddi Jagan, but left the coalition in 1968 and lost ground in the disputed December elections; it now sits in opposition.

The UF is firmly anti-communist, pro-Western and pro-business, defending free enterprise, private property and the Christian churches. Its supporters are Portuguese, Chinese and mixed-race Guyanese, Amerindians of the interior and the Georgetown commercial class. Its leverage lies in money, the Catholic Church and its Western contacts rather than numbers.

2.name: Guyana Bar Association
2.text:
The Guyana Bar Association unites the country's barristers, a profession of great prestige that has produced many of Guyana's politicians across ethnic lines. In 1970 it is the main civic forum where the conduct of the 1968 elections, overseas voting and the coming republican constitution are debated.

Its liberal members defend the rule of law, an independent judiciary, free elections and the rights of the opposition and the press, and are wary of both Burnham's growing power and Jagan's Marxism. With no mass following, its leverage lies in the courts, in legal opinion and in the respect lawyers command in Georgetown society.

3.name: People's National Congress
3.text:
The PNC was founded in 1957 by Forbes Burnham after his break with Cheddi Jagan. Burnham became Premier in 1964 in coalition with the United Force and led Guyana to independence in 1966. The December 1968 elections, marred by charges of fraud in the overseas vote, gave the PNC an outright majority and it now governs alone.

The party draws on Afro-Guyanese voters, the civil service and urban workers. Once favoured by Washington as the alternative to Jagan, it is moving toward 'co-operative socialism', state control of the economy, non-alignment and closer ties with the Third World, and plans to proclaim a Co-operative Republic in February 1970.

4.name: Progressive Youth Organisation
4.text:
The Progressive Youth Organisation is the youth wing of the People's Progressive Party, a school of party cadres who study Marxism-Leninism and are sent on scholarships to the Soviet Union, East Germany and Cuba. It has been active since the 1950s in villages, sugar estates and schools.

The PYO is the most consistently pro-Soviet force in Guyana, pressing the PPP to embrace orthodox communism, which it formally did in 1969. It calls for nationalisation of sugar and bauxite and an alliance with the socialist camp. Its leverage lies in training the next generation of PPP leaders.

5.name: Ratoon
5.text:
Ratoon is a radical group of lecturers and students at the University of Guyana, among them the economist Clive Thomas, which publishes a mimeographed paper of the same name. It belongs to the Caribbean New Left that emerged after the 1968 Rodney riots in Jamaica.

It rejects both Burnham's racial politics and the PPP's Soviet orthodoxy, calling for multiracial working-class unity, workers' control, land reform and a break with foreign ownership of sugar and bauxite. Small but articulate, its leverage lies in the campus, in the regional intellectual network and in young people disillusioned with both big parties.

6.name: African Society for Cultural Relations with Independent Africa
6.english: African Society for Cultural Relations with Independent Africa
6.text:
ASCRIA was founded in 1964 by Eusi Kwayana, formerly Sydney King, to promote African identity, culture and economic self-reliance among Afro-Guyanese. In 1970 it is a close ally of the PNC government, and Kwayana sits on state bodies.

It rejects Western cultural domination, preaches Black consciousness, African dress and names, and wants land and co-operatives for African villagers. Anti-imperialist and drawn to Nkrumah, Nyerere and the African liberation movements, it has strong roots in African villages along the coast. Its leverage lies in its moral authority over the PNC's base, which could turn against the party if it betrays its promises.
6.wiki: African Society for Cultural Relations with Independent Africa

7.name: The Kabaka's Men
7.text:
The Kabaka's Men are the inner circle of loyalists around Forbes Burnham, whom his supporters call 'the Kabaka', after the Ugandan king. They include party organisers, ministers and enforcers who believe the 1968 victory must be made permanent.

They favour a dominant party controlling the state, the army and the unions, election management that leaves nothing to chance, and a foreign policy turning toward Cuba, the Soviet bloc and Third World radicals to shed the image of an American client. Their leverage is the patronage of the ruling party and the leader's personal favour.

8.name: The Tadjah Committees
8.text:
The Tadjah Committees are the village groups that keep alive the Muharram commemoration of the martyrdom of Imam Husayn, brought to Guyana by indentured labourers from India in the nineteenth century. Colonial authorities restricted the processions, and only a few estate communities still build the tadjahs.

Their members cherish a devotional, community-based Shia memory and seek respect for their customs from both the Muslim majority bodies and the state. They have no political ambitions, avoid the PNC-PPP conflict and wield influence only through village festivals and family ties.

9.name: The Karbala Students
9.text:
The Karbala Students are a handful of young Indo-Guyanese Muslims who have encountered Shia teachings through literature from Iraq and Pakistan and dream of studying in the seminaries of Najaf and Karbala. They meet in private homes in Georgetown and on the Corentyne.

They see Husayn's martyrdom as a call to resist injustice, reject both capitalism and communism, and admire clerics who defy secular rulers. Without mosques, money or recognition from Guyana's Sunni bodies, they are a tiny, isolated fringe, but their zeal sets them apart from the quiet devotion of the older generation.

10.name: Guyana United Sad'r Islamic Anjuman
10.text:
The Guyana United Sad'r Islamic Anjuman, founded in 1936, is the oldest national body of Guyanese Muslims, overwhelmingly Sunni and of Indian descent. It runs mosques, Islamic schools, marriage registration and the Eid celebrations that are recognised as national holidays.

It teaches orthodox, politically cautious Islam, keeps on good terms with whichever government is in power and seeks links with Muslim states, scholars and charities abroad. Its leverage lies in the network of mosque committees and the respect of Muslim businessmen and rice farmers.

11.name: The Khilafat Circle
11.text:
The Khilafat Circle is a small study group of young Indo-Guyanese Muslims who take their name from the Indian Khilafat movement of the 1920s and read pan-Islamist pamphlets reaching them from Pakistan and the Middle East.

They argue that Muslims must unite under a restored caliphate, reject secular nationalism, Western culture and Marxism alike, and criticise the established Muslim bodies as too close to politicians. With no organisation beyond a few mosques and homes, they are marginal, but they attract students frustrated by communal politics.

12.name: Guyana United Muslim Party
12.text:
The Guyana United Muslim Party was founded in 1964 to give Guyanese Muslims a political voice of their own, independent of both the PPP and the PNC. It polled poorly and is now largely dormant, but its founders remain respected figures in the Muslim community.

It calls for the defence of Islamic education, recognition of Muslim personal law and festivals, and representation for Muslims in public life, within a democratic and multiracial state. Its leverage lies in community associations and the possibility of trading Muslim votes with the major parties.

13.name: The Co-operative Republic
13.text:
The Co-operative Republic is the project of the planners, lawyers and senior civil servants preparing Guyana's transformation into a republic in February 1970. Their guiding figure is the Attorney General, Shridath Ramphal, who drafts the legal framework.

They believe that co-operatives, state corporations and central planning can make 'the small man a real man', while Guyana steers a non-aligned course between the blocs. Indifferent to ideology and partisan rhetoric, they value administrative control and national ownership. Their leverage lies in the ministries, the treasury and the drafting of laws.

14.name: Guyana Sanatan Dharma Maha Sabha
14.text:
The Maha Sabha is the main body of orthodox Hindus in Guyana, uniting temples, pandits and religious schools among the Indo-Guyanese majority of the coastland and the rice and sugar districts.

It defends Hindu religion, the Hindi language, family and caste customs, and state recognition of Hindu festivals and marriages. Socially conservative and wary of both Marxist atheism and Afro-Guyanese dominance of the state, it leans toward the PPP's voters yet guards its independence. Its leverage lies in the pandits' authority over village life and their ability to sway Indian votes.

15.name: Booker McConnell
15.text:
Booker McConnell is the British conglomerate that owns most of Guyana's sugar estates, as well as shops, shipping and rum distilleries, so dominant that the colony was once called 'Booker's Guiana'. Under Sir Jock Campbell it reformed its labour practices and promoted local managers.

Its interests lie in security of property, stable labour relations and a government that avoids nationalisation. Together with the bauxite giants Demerara Bauxite (Alcan) and Reynolds, it controls the bulk of exports and foreign exchange. Its leverage over jobs, revenue and London is immense, though it is the obvious target of any socialist programme.

16.name: Georgetown Chamber of Commerce
16.text:
The Georgetown Chamber of Commerce, dating back to the nineteenth century, represents the merchants, importers and small manufacturers of the capital, many of them Portuguese, Chinese and Indian family businesses.

It defends free enterprise, low taxation, open trade and security of property, and grows uneasy as the government speaks of co-operative socialism and state trading. It favours good relations with the United States, Britain and Canada as sources of credit and investment. Its leverage lies in its members' control of retail trade and their access to ministers.

17.name: The Kaieteur Guardians
17.text:
The Kaieteur Guardians are the naturalists, museum staff, foresters and teachers who champion Kaieteur National Park, established in 1929 around one of the world's highest single-drop waterfalls, and the protection of Guyana's vast interior rainforest.

They warn against reckless logging, gold and diamond mining and hydroelectric schemes, and call for the rights of Amerindian communities to be respected. Few in number and without party ties, they rely on scientific credibility, the national pride attached to Kaieteur and contacts with international scientific bodies.

18.name: People's Progressive Party
18.text:
The People's Progressive Party, founded in 1950 by Cheddi and Janet Jagan, led the anti-colonial struggle and governed until 1964, when it was removed under a new electoral system amid strikes and riots backed by Britain and the United States. It denounces the 1968 elections as rigged and remains the main opposition.

In 1969 the PPP declared itself a Marxist-Leninist party and aligned with the Soviet Union. It calls for nationalisation of sugar and bauxite, land reform and an end to foreign domination. Its base is Indo-Guyanese sugar workers and rice farmers, and its leverage lies in the sugar unions.

19.name: Working People's Vanguard Party
19.text:
The Working People's Vanguard Party was formed by Brindley Benn, former Deputy Premier and chairman of the PPP, after his break with Cheddi Jagan in the late 1960s. Benn accuses the PPP of reformism and of following Moscow's revisionist line.

The party takes its inspiration from Mao Zedong and the Chinese revolution, calling for armed struggle, peasant mobilisation and a united front of Indian and African workers against imperialism and the comprador class. It is small and largely Georgetown-based, with its leverage limited to radical youth and Benn's personal reputation.

20.name: The Rupununi Ranchers
20.text:
The Rupununi Ranchers are the cattle-owning families of the southern savannahs, among them the Harts and Melvilles, who led the Rupununi uprising of January 1969 against the Burnham government, with arms and support from Venezuela. The army crushed the revolt and the leaders fled across the border.

They demand autonomy for the interior, security of land titles against government plans and protection from Georgetown's politicians. Anti-communist and suspicious of Afro-Guyanese and Indo-Guyanese rule alike, they have ties to some Amerindian communities and to Venezuelan officials, who use them in the border dispute.

21.name: The 1964 Squads
21.text:
The 1964 Squads are the veterans of the armed communal gangs that terrorised villages during the racial disturbances of 1962 to 1964, when arson, bombings and killings drove Indians and Africans apart and left hundreds dead or homeless.

They see politics as a war between races, preach armed self-defence and dominance for their own group, and despise compromise and multiracial appeals. Without a recognised organisation, they survive as networks of hardened men in certain villages and ports, available to anyone wishing to stir communal fear.

22.name: Guyana Defence Force
22.text:
The Guyana Defence Force was formed in 1965 from the British Guiana Volunteer Force and the Special Service Unit, and took over from British troops at independence. Its officers were trained at Sandhurst and Mons, and its first test came in crushing the Rupununi uprising of January 1969.

The force is small but loyal to the government, and its ranks are predominantly Afro-Guyanese. It guards the disputed borders with Venezuela and Suriname, and Burnham is careful to bind it closely to the ruling party. Its leverage lies in its monopoly of arms and its role in any internal crisis.

23.name: Monarchy of Guyana
23.text:
Since independence in 1966, Queen Elizabeth II has been Queen of Guyana, represented in Georgetown by a Governor-General, Sir Edward Luckhoo since the death of Sir David Rose in late 1969. The Crown's days are numbered, as the government plans to proclaim a republic on 23 February 1970.

The monarchy's remaining supporters are older civil servants, Anglican and Catholic clergy, and parts of the Portuguese, Chinese and mixed-race middle class who value continuity, the Commonwealth tie and a neutral head of state above the racial divide. They have no party of their own, only tradition and sentiment.
